title: Protest, policing and rights: organisers on changing law and practice
label: 28 October 2026 · Security, safety and protest
summary: Organisers from Save British Farming, Palestine Solidarity Campaign and Southall Black Sisters told the committee police use more conditions and new laws are creating legal uncertainty and a chilling effect on protest. Experiences differed—farmers described constructive liaison because of vehicle protests, Palestine solidarity organisers described frequent short‑notice restrictions and route bans, and Southall Black Sisters emphasised historic bias and the extra risks faced by non‑citizens. All three urged rolling back or clarifying restrictive powers and said police should prioritise facilitation over suppression.

chapters.title: What changed in policing of protests
chapters.takeaway: Organisers say police use of conditions and new powers has increased and often limits protest activity, producing a chilling effect.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. You have all run protests recently; have you noticed any change in police actions?

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: Yes. Over the last three years we've seen routine use of public order powers to impose conditions—on times, routes and even where we may assemble. Often police agree a plan and then impose conditions days later that make it risky to overrun or deviate.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Have those technical breaches led to arrests for running over time?

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: Not for overrunning time in our experience, but people have been arrested for being on the 'wrong side of the road' when conditions said otherwise. The real effect is chilling: speakers cut short, people deterred from speaking.

turns.speaker: Liz Webster
turns.text: Our experience was different. In 2020 the police were cautious because of Covid and tractors were new in London. By 2024–25 we’d built a working relationship; with vehicle protests we had more practical liaison and fewer confrontations.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Did you face the same pressures about time limits or being moved on?

turns.speaker: Liz Webster
turns.text: There are legal differences for moving-vehicle protests. We tried to comply with police requests because we didn't want farmers arrested and wanted the message to get through without creating danger for London services.

turns.speaker: Rahila Gupta
turns.text: I want to broaden this: policing of protests sits within a history of biased policing. For racialised communities that history makes us wary. We also fear the legal changes give police tools they didn't have before, and that alters who feels safe to protest.

chapters.title: Liaison, trust and practical planning
chapters.takeaway: Organisers do pre-event liaison but say police sometimes refuse genuine dialogue, imposing last‑minute conditions that prevent legal challenge.

turns.speaker: Afzal Khan
turns.text: Do you see police as facilitators or obstacles, and have you changed your approach?

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: We always notify police and want safe, stewarded marches, but increasingly police use powers to curtail protests. We’ve been banned from sites like the BBC and have had megaphones outlawed at short notice—making stewarding and safety harder.

turns.speaker: Liz Webster
turns.text: I chose a cooperative route: I met Met officers, explained aims, and worked with them. That built trust and made things smoother. Organising in London is heavy responsibility—you're dealing with big machines, traffic and public safety.

turns.speaker: Rahila Gupta
turns.text: For some people the risk is higher. Non‑citizens worry about immigration consequences. Proposals like 'earned settlement' and good‑character tests mean cautions or convictions can affect someone's right to remain—so they face extra deterrents.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lane-Fox of Soho
turns.text: Peter, you sounded mistrustful of some liaison groups. How do your pre‑event meetings work, and what stops trust?

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: It varies. Sometimes senior officials publicly criticise our marches. Operationally, police have refused to meet unless we accept their proposed route, or they threaten to impose unknown conditions days before the event, leaving us no time to challenge decisions.

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: Short notice conditions disincentivise proper dialogue. If police know they can impose conditions without scrutiny, they have less reason to engage in good‑faith planning with organisers.

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: My solution: more pressure on police to fulfil the duty to facilitate lawful protest rather than default to restriction.

chapters.title: Laws, powers and suggested changes
chapters.takeaway: All three witnesses urge scrutiny or repeal of recent anti‑protest laws and fewer reactive new offences; police should be properly resourced instead.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lane-Fox of Soho
turns.text: Have recent laws made it clearer when protest is unlawful? What single change would you ask for?

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: The law now allows many ways to prevent effective protest. The proscription of Palestine Action was chilling. I'd start by revisiting the Crime and Policing Act and other anti‑protest measures that enable suppression rather than facilitation.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lane-Fox of Soho
turns.text: Liz, your view?

turns.speaker: Liz Webster
turns.text: I worry about kneejerk legislating that makes the police's job box‑ticking and drives us toward an illiberal state. My ask would be: step back from creating more offences, properly fund policing, and open better routes for public petitions so people feel heard without confrontation.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lane-Fox of Soho
turns.text: Rahila, what would you change in the law if you could?

turns.speaker: Rahila Gupta
turns.text: Repeal a lot of the newer powers: serious disruption prevention orders, excessive-noise clauses, and restrictions that curb the theatre of protest. Police already have strong tools; extra laws have made policing disproportionate.

turns.speaker: Baroness Chakrabarti
turns.text: If a supporter is nervous about joining a march, what do you tell them?

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: I understand the fear—students, refugees, people on visas worry. Arrests at our events are relatively rare, but the fear is real. We encourage participation because protests have shifted policy before, but people should weigh personal risks, and organisers should make events as safe as possible.

turns.speaker: Liz Webster
turns.text: I tell people organising protests is a big responsibility. If you want to reduce protests, give citizens stronger, more direct routes to Parliament so people feel heard without feeling they must resort to disruptive action.

chapters.title: Noise, routes and identity
chapters.takeaway: Restrictions on noise, routes and face coverings affect the style and safety of protests; examples include bans on megaphones and demands to remove masks.

turns.speaker: Lord Rook
turns.text: Have rules about excessive noise changed how you act?

turns.speaker: Rahila Gupta
turns.text: We still bring megaphones and drums because the spirit of protest is singing and chanting. But the threat of enforcement creates a chilling effect—people worry when police will intervene.

turns.speaker: Liz Webster
turns.text: Police told us not to blow horns near Parliament Square early on. Protests involve theatre and noise; bans can blunt a demonstration. We tried to cooperate, but heavy‑handed responses early on felt disproportionate.

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: Examples: we were banned from banging pots when famine was declared in Gaza, and banned from megaphones during a state visit. Those rules silenced effective protest on moments that mattered.

turns.speaker: Lord Murray of Blidworth
turns.text: Has the 'cumulative disruption' test in the 2026 Act affected you?

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: Yes. 'Cumulative disruption' is vague and has been used to deny routes or sites—like the BBC—by referencing past protests. That creates a loop: restrictions push us to fewer routes, which then gets used to justify more restriction.

turns.speaker: Lord Murray of Blidworth
turns.text: Have you changed how you plan as a result?

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: We have tried to vary routes, but police conditions have narrowed our choices and prevented marches where we'd most want to be heard.

chapters.title: New offences, stop‑search and masks
chapters.takeaway: New offences and stop‑search powers mostly create a deterrent atmosphere; rules on concealing identity have practical and unequal impacts.

turns.speaker: Euan Stainbank
turns.text: Do newer offences like 'locking on' or targeting infrastructure affect your events?

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: Not directly—we don't plan direct action—but these offences contribute to a climate that labels protest more dangerous and risky. The proscription of Palestine Action is an example of that chilling effect.

turns.speaker: Liz Webster
turns.text: I actively steer people away from disruptive or destructive tactics—farmers want sympathy and public support, not criminal records. If people feel unheard, though, there is always a risk some will escalate.

turns.speaker: Rahila Gupta
turns.text: Anecdote: my partner was arrested for holding a sign supporting Palestine Action. I had to step back from some activism to protect our organisation. People pick and choose risks depending on jobs, visas and family responsibilities.

turns.speaker: Lord Murray of Blidworth
turns.text: The 2023 power to stop and search for protest tools—has that been used against you?

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: We're not aware of searches for things like glue, but the fact that protesters face different stop‑search rules feeds the sense that protestors have fewer protections and that this will put people off attending.

turns.speaker: Lord Rook
turns.text: How about laws on concealing identity—masks and face coverings?

turns.speaker: Rahila Gupta
turns.text: That hits our women hard. Some wore Covid masks because they feared being filmed; police demanded removal and one woman said she felt unsafe and might not come again. At the same time, men in black at counter‑protests were not challenged—there's inconsistency and it chills participation.

turns.speaker: Liz Webster
turns.text: It even affects theatre: we like to dress up as animals at demos, and face‑covering rules complicate that. Laws made as reactions end up restricting harmless, expressive protest culture.

chapters.title: Balancing free speech, safety and the moratorium debate
chapters.takeaway: All witnesses want a careful distinction between offensive speech and threats; organisers steward events, social media and counter‑protest filming drive policing, and calls to pause pro‑Palestine marches were strongly opposed.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: Where should the line be between upsetting speech and unlawful threatening speech, and who should act when the line is crossed?

turns.speaker: Rahila Gupta
turns.text: The issue is politicised. Arrests for slogans like 'Globalise the Intifada' sit beside arrests for racial abuse aimed at Black police officers. The law risks treating very different harms as the same. We should be cautious about expanding 'offence' to cover mere upset.

turns.speaker: Liz Webster
turns.text: Language can be dangerous—I have a family experience of racial violence—but over‑legislating to catch every offensive word is the wrong route. Focus on serious threats and protecting communities rather than policing every insult.

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: Freedom of speech needs nuance: political statements that some find offensive should not be treated as criminal unless they incite violence or hatred. We've seen inconsistency—for example, Arabic words being treated differently from English equivalents.

turns.speaker: Euan Stainbank
turns.text: Is social media and filming by counter‑protesters altering policing priorities?

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: Yes. Counter‑protesters often film demonstrations searching for items they can report to police; police sometimes respond to social media pressure rather than events on the ground. That skews enforcement and creates perverse incentives.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: Organisers—do you see preventing abusive speech as part of your role?

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: We have stewarding, clear anti‑racism messaging and stewards challenge wrongdoing where they can, but stewards have limits. The police must protect rights; organisers can help but can't replace policing.

turns.speaker: Liz Webster
turns.text: Organisers can't control every attendee. If a far‑right group turns up uninvited, we can't always manage that. Responsibility is shared—organisers, police and, where relevant, community leaders.

turns.speaker: Rahila Gupta
turns.text: Also beware turning 'offence' into 'incitement to hatred'—we've become over‑sensitive in ways that could criminalise normal political argument.

turns.speaker: Afzal Khan
turns.text: The independent reviewer suggested a moratorium on pro‑Palestine marches over antisemitism concerns—how do you respond?

turns.speaker: Peter Leary
turns.text: That conflates protests with unrelated acts of violence and risks equating criticism of Israeli state policy with hatred of Jewish people. Many Jewish people march with us; the Nakba Day march is a solemn commemoration. A moratorium would reward far‑right attempts to silence us and wrongly criminalise political dissent.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. That closes the session—thanks to all witnesses for their detailed, direct evidence.
